content.content:
1	<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->
2	
3	# Facts on record
4	
5	## Execution model
6	
7	- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
8	- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library, so by default it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command, which follows the selection (F-381); under the selection, `f(i: Index)` passes the check (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
9	- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
10	- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
11	- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
12	- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
13	- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
14	- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). Under walk, `Vector` and `Matrix` take their sizes from an array built at run time: `f[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\])` takes `s` from `array[\RR64\](3)`, and overloads on `Vector` and `Matrix` dispatch by rank (row 214). The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). Source: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:96`.
15	- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). Both paths stop at a syntax error at `excludes`, since an object has no `excludes` clause (measured: `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, E4). Without that clause, both report `T is undefined` at the `T` of the `extends` clause: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as row 17 holds for a trait. Today's specification refuses the form in any case, by instantiation exclusion, and marks it "Not allowed" beside the parametric `Nothing[\T\]` that the interpreter's library writes (F-167). P-90 still calls the bare `Nothing` future work that waits for such `where` clauses, not tried before then. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
16	- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".
17	- F-23 **A comment placed after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span and of the unambiguous name the parser derives from it.** The parser's `createSpan` trims back over spaces only, and a declaration that ends in `end` is unaffected (row 359). 42	- F-37 **On the compiled path, a `typecase` clause on a sized type, such as `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]`, tests the value's own class, also when the size is a static parameter of the enclosing function.** The test is one `INSTANCEOF` on the class of the instantiation, `Vec⟦FZZ32,3⟧`. In a generic function, the class loader puts in the size when it makes the function's instance. So a `typecase` tells `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]` from `Vec[\ZZ32,4\]`, and does not read the descriptor that a size has (P-41). No live declaration of the one library has an `opr` static parameter: `FortressLibrary`'s two, in `embiggen` and `Monoid`, are inside comments. 52	- F-47 **The exclusion rule refuses some of the specification's own examples; in their place, a parametric object with a factory, or a widening function, runs on both paths as a user program.** The refused examples are E1 to E10 of `reviews/spec-refused-examples.md`, "What was found": among them three `where`-clause examples, the Working Draft's `Nothing`, the nested number tower and `RationalQuantity`. Detail: `reviews/spec-refused-examples-judgement.md` section 6.

56	- F-51 **A generic call converts a narrower argument for a parameter typed by a type variable that another argument fixes, on both paths.** For `scale[\T\](b: Box[\T\], x: T)` and `b: Box[\RR64\]`, `scale(b, 3)` takes `T = RR64` and converts the `3` (row 388, fixed). Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK` and `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review/row388-container-probe.md`.

Measured by the note's probes, which `84aef6a4f` removed (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways/Q3*.txt` in its parent). Detail: `reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md`, "Question 3", section 2.

<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->

# Facts on record

## Execution model

- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library, so by default it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command, which follows the selection (F-381); under the selection, `f(i: Index)` passes the check (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team left two separate traces for unboxing. The plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java` lists what to unbox: a primitive, a singleton object, unboxed fields, and a `comprises` clause whose types are unboxable; it says nothing of the loader or of instantiations. The loader has an empty "expando" stub (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). A loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; joins: F-350); it counts no call in the prelude's files (row 982) or of a function declared later in the file (row 987). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range into chunks of at most 16 elements (F-350), and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1498-1585`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129).
